## Solution

Let $\xi \sim N(0, I_d)$ and let $B$ be symmetric positive definite. We wish to determine for which $d \ge 1$ the expectation
$$\mathrm{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{\xi^{\top} B\,\xi}\right]$$
is finite.

**Diagonalization.** Since $B$ is symmetric positive definite, there exists an orthogonal matrix $O$ such that
$$O^{\top} B\, O = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_d), \qquad \lambda_i > 0.$$
Set $\eta = O^{\top}\xi$. Since $O$ is orthogonal and $\xi$ has law $N(0,I_d)$, the vector $\eta$ is again $N(0,I_d)$, with independent standard Gaussian coordinates $\eta_1,\dots,\eta_d$. Moreover
$$\xi^{\top} B\,\xi = \eta^{\top}\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_i)\,\eta = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \lambda_i\,\eta_i^{2}.$$
Thus the problem reduces to the finiteness of
$$\mathrm{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_i\eta_i^{2}}\right], \qquad \eta_i \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1),\ \lambda_i>0.$$

**Polar coordinates.** Write $\eta = r\,\theta$ with $r = \|\eta\| \ge 0$ and $\theta \in S^{d-1}$. The Lebesgue measure becomes $d\eta = r^{d-1}\,dr\,d\sigma(\theta)$, where $d\sigma$ is the surface measure on the unit sphere. The quadratic form factors as
$$\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_i\eta_i^{2} = r^{2}\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_i\theta_i^{2}}_{=:\,q(\theta)} = r^{2}\,q(\theta).$$
Because $B$ is positive definite, $q(\theta) = \theta^{\top}B\theta \ge \lambda_{\min}(B) > 0$ for every unit vector $\theta$, so $1/q(\theta)$ is a bounded, continuous function on the compact set $S^{d-1}$.

The Gaussian density of $\eta$ is $(2\pi)^{-d/2}e^{-\|\eta\|^{2}/2}$, which is bounded above and bounded below (by a positive constant) on every ball $B_\varepsilon$ around the origin. Hence the finiteness of the expectation is governed, up to harmless bounded factors, by the integral
$$\int_{B_\varepsilon}\frac{d\eta}{\sum_i\lambda_i\eta_i^{2}} \;=\; \int_{S^{d-1}}\frac{d\sigma(\theta)}{q(\theta)}\int_{0}^{\varepsilon} r^{d-3}\,dr.$$

**Radial integral.** The angular integral is finite (the integrand is bounded). The radial integral
$$\int_{0}^{\varepsilon} r^{d-3}\,dr$$
converges if and only if $d - 3 > -1$, i.e. $d > 2$, equivalently $d \ge 3$.

- For $d = 1$: $\int_{0}^{\varepsilon} r^{-2}\,dr = +\infty$.
- For $d = 2$: $\int_{0}^{\varepsilon} r^{-1}\,dr = +\infty$ (logarithmic divergence).
- For $d \ge 3$: $\int_{0}^{\varepsilon} r^{d-3}\,dr = \dfrac{\varepsilon^{d-2}}{d-2} < \infty$.

**Away from the origin.** For $\|\eta\| \ge \varepsilon$,
$$\sum_i \lambda_i \eta_i^{2} \ge \lambda_{\min}(B)\,\|\eta\|^{2} \ge \lambda_{\min}(B)\,\varepsilon^{2} > 0,$$
so $1/(\sum_i\lambda_i\eta_i^{2})$ is bounded there, and the integral over $\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus B_\varepsilon$ is finite for every $d \ge 1$.

**Conclusion.** Combining both regions, $\mathrm{E}\!\left[(\xi^{\top}B\xi)^{-1}\right]$ is finite if and only if $d \ge 3$. The threshold is independent of the particular positive definite matrix $B$ (the angular factor is always finite; only the radial exponent $d-3$ matters).

$$\boxed{\,d \ge 3\,}$$
